newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia studies plywood futures, palm oil options.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia studies plywood futures, palm oil options.

text.p: Malaysia has started a study on introducing plywood futures on the Kuala Lumpur Commodities Exchange (KLCE) and plans to follow through with palm oil options, KLCE acting chief Raghbir Bhart said on Monday.
"A feasibility study was started just last week on the plywood futures and we'll know the results in four to five months," Bhart told Reuters in a telephone interview.
He said the study was being conducted by an official of the United Nations Commisssion of Trade and Development (UNCTAD).

"We may have another study later for the palm oil options," he said, adding they could not foresee any problems in introducing the new products on the KLCE if the studies proved the instruments were viable.
"The trading mechanisms, legislative structures are all in place. It'll just be another product," he said.
Timber industry officials said plywood futures would provide stability to both the commodity and the KLCE.

"We have long waited for a local market to trade plywood futures and are looking forward to this," said Sarawak Timber Association manager Barney Chan. "The KLCE will also have a wider base of products."
Sarawak, a Malaysian state on Borneo island, is home to the country's largest timber resources.
Chan said Malaysia currently exported about 4.5 million cubic metres of plywood annually.
"This is sufficent to sustain supply for a futures trade in plywood," he said.
Palm oil traders also welcomed the proposed palm oil options but doubted the feasibility of the plan.
"Options are a very new thing in Malaysia and I'm worried whether the liquidity in the current market can sustain such contracts," said a trader.
Palm oil dealers said the average daily volume transacted on the KLCE was now between 2,500-3,000 futures lots or 62,500-75,000 tonnes.
"I think it'll be a very good counter that could see a lot of trading once it takes off," said another trader. "But we're going to need a lot of support from the plantations."
